title: Threat Modeling: the design under attack
description: STRIDE, data flow diagrams and risk prioritization: finding the flaws on the whiteboard, when fixing them still costs zero.

1.title: STRIDE over the data flow diagram
1.body:
## The method in 4 questions

1. **What are we building?** → the DFD.
2. **What can go wrong?** → STRIDE over each element.
3. **What are we going to do about it?** → mitigate/accept/transfer.
4. **Did we do a good job?** → validate and repeat on every iteration.

## The minimal DFD of a web app

```
[User]   ──HTTPS──▶ (API) ──▶ [Postgres]
[Admin]  ──HTTPS──▶ (API) ──▶ [S3 bucket]
                        └────▶ [External payments API]
```

Each **element** of the DFD has its natural threats — that's where
STRIDE comes in, as a checklist:

| DFD element | STRIDE letters that apply |
|---|---|
| Data flow | T (tampering), I (interception), D |
| Process (API) | All of STRIDE |
| Data store (DB/S3) | T, I, R (audit logs), D |
| External entity | S (spoofing) |

## STRIDE translated into real attacks

Each category has an offensive room where you will exploit it. Most of them are in the
Jr Penetration Tester and Web Application Pentesting paths: come back to this table when
you complete them and you'll see the same knowledge from the other side.

| Letter | Question | Room where you'll practice it |
|---|---|---|
| **S**poofing | Can I pass myself off as someone else? | auth-bypass, session-security |
| **T**ampering | Can I modify data in transit/at rest? | jwt-security (alg none) |
| **R**epudiation | Can I deny my action? (no logs) | log-forging (just the opposite) |
| **I**nformation disclosure | Can I see what I shouldn't? | BOLA (api-security), sqli |
| **D**enial of service | Can I take the service down? | api-security (unlimited consumption) |
| **E**levation of privilege | Can I escalate? | mass-assignment, privesc-linux |

The teaching revelation: every offensive room on this platform IS an
executed threat model. Designing with STRIDE is writing the attack BEFORE
the attacker does — literally the same knowledge, on the other side of
the whiteboard.

threat-modeling-t01-q01.prompt: What does a DFD (Data Flow Diagram) represent and what are its 4 standard elements?
threat-modeling-t01-q01.hint: It's the map of where the data moves: who sends it, who transforms it, where it is stored and through which channels it travels.

options.a: The physical network: routers, switches, firewalls and servers
options.b: The system map: processes, data stores, external entities and data flows
options.c: The class model: classes, attributes, methods and relationships
options.d: The risk matrix: threats, impacts, likelihoods and controls

threat-modeling-t01-q02.prompt: What do the 6 letters of STRIDE stand for?
threat-modeling-t01-q02.hint: Each letter is a threat category; review the "STRIDE translated into real attacks" table.

options.a: Scanning, Tracing, Rootkits, Injection, DDoS, Exfiltration
options.b: Sniffing, Trojans, Replay, Interception, DNS poisoning, Escalation
options.c: Spoofing, Tampering, Ransomware, Intrusion, Defacement, Exploitation
options.d: Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information disclosure, Denial of service, Elevation of privilege

threat-modeling-t01-q03.prompt: An attacker modifies an order in transit between the browser and the API. Which STRIDE letter is it?
threat-modeling-t01-q03.hint: Tampering — without HTTPS/integrity, the data flow is the target

threat-modeling-t01-q04.prompt: Logs stored WITHOUT identifying the user/IP/time open up which STRIDE category?
threat-modeling-t01-q04.hint: Repudiation: the attacker can deny having done it — without binding evidence there is no attribution

2.title: Prioritize risks and embed it in the SDLC
2.body:
## From the list of threats to the list of tasks

A threat modeling meeting produces 30 threats; the month has 40 hours. You
prioritize. **DREAD** scores each threat 1-10 on five axes (Damage,
Reproducibility, Exploitability, Affected users, Discoverability) and the
average orders the list. Today many teams directly use
Impact × Likelihood or a mapping to CVSS.

With the list sorted, each threat gets one of FOUR decisions:

| Decision | When | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Mitigate** | Cost of the control < risk | HTTPS everywhere (T/I) |
| **Accept** | Low risk or disproportionate cost | Public rating without login |
| **Transfer** | Someone else covers it better | WAF/CDN anti-DDoS to the provider |
| **Avoid** | The feature isn't worth the risk | Disable file uploads |

The important part: the decision is WRITTEN DOWN with its justification and an owner.
"We'll look into it" is not a category.

## Threat modeling in the real cycle

It's not a one-off ceremony: it lives with the product.

```
new design    ──▶  threat modeling session (1-2h, team + security)
                        │
                        ▼
              threats → backlog issues (with priority)
                        │
        ┌───────────────┴───────────────┐
        ▼                               ▼
  sprint: controls               review: new features
  (tests that prove them)         = new threats? repeat
```

Signs that you're doing it right: pentest findings
**stop being a surprise** (they were already in the model), security
requirements reach the backlog as normal user stories, and the repo's
DFD is as up to date as the README.

## Other frameworks (in case you run into them)

- **PASTA** (7 steps, oriented to business risk — heavier).
- **LINDDUN** (privacy: the STRIDE of personal data).
- **Attack trees** (from the offensive side: break a goal down into
  attack paths — fits perfectly with the mindset of the offensive
  rooms).

The framework matters less than the habit: looking at the system like the
attacker, on every iteration, with a written record of what was decided.
Everything else is just picking the checklist.

threat-modeling-t02-q01.prompt: What is the classic formulation of risk (the multiplication used by DREAD and almost every model)?
threat-modeling-t02-q01.hint: It combines how much damage the threat would do with how likely it is to happen. DREAD breaks it down into Damage, Reproducibility, Exploitability, Affected users and Discoverability.

options.b: Risk = Cost of the control × Number of assets

threat-modeling-t02-q02.prompt: What are the 4 possible responses to an identified risk (the classic management quadrant)?
threat-modeling-t02-q02.hint: It's the same framework as in business risk; review the decision table in this task.

threat-modeling-t02-q03.prompt: In which SDLC phase is threat modeling cheapest and most effective?
threat-modeling-t02-q03.hint: Design (before the code): fixing it in design = hours; in production = incidents + patches + reputation
